Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend on their way to the airport calls, thinking they left their passport at home, and asks if you can check and bring it to them right away.
Expectation2: Participate in civic life by staying informed, voting, and giving constructive feedback
Situation2: An online candidate forum for their district is streaming now.
Story:
I was just settling in with my laptop, ready to watch the live candidate forum for my district. I’d been looking forward to it all week—this election felt important, and I wanted to be an informed voter, maybe even ask a question in the chat. Just as the opening statements began, my phone buzzed. It was Sam, my oldest friend, sounding frantic. “I think I left my passport at home! I’m almost at the airport. Can you check and bring it if it’s there? Please, I’ll miss my flight otherwise.”

My heart pounded. As a friend, I knew Sam would do the same for me—drop everything in an emergency. But as a citizen, I felt a responsibility to participate in this forum, to listen and maybe even influence the discussion. The candidates were already introducing themselves. I stared at my phone, torn. Sam’s voice echoed in my mind, desperate and trusting, while the forum’s chat scrolled by, full of questions I wanted to ask. I felt pulled in two directions, the weight of both roles pressing on me, unsure which expectation I should meet.
